items.title: SkillSentry: Adaptive Honey Worlds for Dynamic Safety Testing of Agent Skills
items.summary: SkillSentry is a dynamic safety-testing framework that uses adaptive honey worlds to probe LLM agent skills for conditional, execution-time harms. It infers a skill’s intended capability boundary, builds an LLM-simulated environment with controlled decoy resources, adaptively generates tasks, and contrasts skill-enabled trajectories with matched no-skill runs, attributing suspicious behaviors to code and verified traces before deciding. Evaluated against seven scanner configurations, it attains 99.50% Recall and 96.26% average F1 on standard benchmarks, and 92.95% average F1 under semantics-preserving evasion versus 80.07% for the strongest baselines.
items.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, attribution-grounded dynamic testing approach that outperforms static/one-shot scanners, relevant for securing tool-augmented agents and adversarial evaluation pipelines.
items.reason: Directly addresses dynamic, conditional attack surfaces of external agent skills with a proactive adaptive testing/honeypot approach—highly relevant to red-teaming and agent tooling attack surfaces.

items.title: Gradient Immunity: Null-Space Resistance to Malicious Fine-Tuning
items.summary: The paper targets the PPOW setting where most weights are trainable but a small safety-critical component is preserved, and proposes a Unidirectional Safety Gate implemented as a Null Space Cubic Layer plus an Inverse Adapter after the final Transformer layer. The cubic layer blocks or suppresses gradients from harmful samples whose hidden states lie within a calibrated protected region (threshold set using defender-held harmful data), while the Inverse Adapter restores the base model’s forward behavior. Across six model–dataset settings, this keeps post-finetuning attack success near pre-release levels under a fixed threshold, maintains high safe-pass on easier settings, and shows a clearer safety–utility trade-off on BeaverTails unsafe samples, indicating release-time representation-space blocking can raise the cost of malicious adaptation without downstream cooperation.
items.why_it_matters: Offers a concrete, release-time gradient-blocking mechanism that preserves forward behavior while resisting malicious fine-tuning—relevant to robust alignment under open-weight releases and complementary to gradient/representation-control methods in LLM safety.
items.reason: Direct defense proposal against malicious fine-tuning of released weights (PPOW setting) — highly relevant to LLM security, supply-chain attacks, and robustness of deployed models.

items.title: GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning

llm-security.title: HarnessSafe: Evaluating Safety Across Persistent Carriers in Agent Harnesses

llm-security.summary: The paper introduces a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework to create dynamic security baselines for RENs, addressing the challenge that elephant flows resemble volumetric attacks to conventional monitors. llm-security.title: When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on self-evolving skill (SES) systems that distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, where an attacker with skill-level black-box access contributes bounded evidence to influence skill promotion. It formalizes artifact poisoning as requiring Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization, identifying Attribution—making target behaviors appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable—as the key bottleneck, and demonstrates high success embedding target behaviors across six LLM evolvers in SkillClaw (91.0% SER) and transfer to Trace2Skill (61.5% SER) at 10% attacker support. Controlled studies show three consistent attacker records in a 30-record batch suffice while one is much weaker, and ablations highlight recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as main success factors, framing evidence promotion as a critical security boundary for self-evolving agents.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It pinpoints the promotion/attribution step in skill evolution as an attack surface with quantified vulnerability and transferable effects, informing defenses for agentic LLMs and data-driven skill distillation pipelines.
llm-security.reason: Robust context-aware segmentation for malicious instructions (IPI) targets detection of embedded prompt injections tailored to a query—highly relevant to defending agents and evaluating instruction-level attacks.

llm-security.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.
llm-security.reason: Directly studies information leakage from PEFT adapters in public-base services — highly relevant to model extraction, PIi leakage, and red-team measurement for LLM security.

llm-security.summary: The paper introduces LoRAScan, an adapter-aware defense that detects and rejects trigger-bearing inputs for potentially backdoored LoRA adapters at inference time without modifying adapter parameters. llm-security.title: Policy-Masked Private Experts: Auditable and Reversible Capability Access Control in Sparse MoE Models
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Policy-Masked Private Experts, which freeze a pretrained sparse MoE, train a disjoint private expert branch, and use policy-controlled pool selection before top-k routing to ensure unauthorized requests execute no private experts under the stated TCB. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite show zero unauthorized private execution across 64 adversarial scenarios and 96 deny/fail-closed events with exact hook agreement and reversible allow-deny-allow behavior, while private branches yield significant gains on frozen Qwen benchmarks and 27.0 pp on DeepSeek, and outperform LoRA plus post-hoc gating in preventing denied adapter calls. A sealed evaluation is near-neutral, and the authors emphasize that execution control is auditable and reversible, though transfer utility remains distribution dependent.

llm-security.title: Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models
llm-security.summary: The work argues that standard NTP’s teacher-forced training is suboptimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning, and that existing MTP and NextLat objectives either have limited horizons or suffer from compounding rollout errors. It proposes Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), introducing an auxiliary higher-level abstract latent to reduce error accumulation in latent-space rollouts. Experiments indicate HiLP yields longer-horizon coherent belief state representations, improves performance on coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks, and enables more efficient speculative decoding.
llm-security.why_it_matters: HiLP targets long-horizon error accumulation with a hierarchical latent rollout, offering a potentially practical auxiliary objective for robust reasoning and faster decoding compared to MTP/NextLat baselines.
llm-security.reason: Fast, gradient-free one-shot unlearning for LLMs targets removal of sensitive data/PII and addresses practical security/privacy needs; potential for incomplete removal and attack/restore vectors makes it highly relevant.

llm-security.title: Skill-Use: Can LLMs Actually Use Skills in Agentic Harnesses?
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Skill-Use, a benchmark that tests whether LLM agents can recognize, retrieve, and apply structured skills under progressive disclosure, separating Trigger, Compliance, and Boundary facets and combining them into an SU score that only credits execution after triggering. It comprises 79 real skills and 177 executable tasks across nine domains, run in Docker sandboxes and scored via trajectory-based rubrics, and evaluates eight LLMs across two agent harnesses. Results show reliable skill use is not yet achieved (best SU 0.613), with triggering and procedural compliance as independent bottlenecks and scores/model rankings varying by harness, indicating skill use is harness-conditioned rather than an inherent model property.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, execution-grounded way to diagnose harness-conditioned failure modes (triggering vs. compliance vs. boundary) in tool-using LLM agents, informing both security-sensitive agent design and modular capability evaluation akin to time-series foundation model benchmarking.
llm-security.reason: Skill-Use evaluates whether agents can recognize and retrieve procedural skills under partial disclosure—directly relevant to agentic systems, tool-use security surfaces and evaluation methodology for skill-based attacks/robustness.

llm-security.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. llm-security.title: Evaluation Pitfalls and Sparsity Limitations in LLM-based Confidence Estimates for Classification
llm-security.summary: The paper finds that common LLM confidence verbalization for classification is extremely sparse, e.g., Qwen3-32B yields only eight unique values on SST-2 with over half at exactly 95%, a pattern repeated across four datasets and two LLMs. This sparsity skews evaluation: AUARC rankings change drastically depending on interpolation choice, with consistency sampling dropping from best to worst under stepwise vs. linear interpolation, motivating a call to standardize stepwise interpolation. Under this fairer evaluation, “verbalization logprobs,” which weights verbalized digits by token probabilities, mitigates sparsity and yields the best AUARC, improving by 2.3 points over vanilla verbalization without extra inference cost.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It highlights a pervasive sparsity artifact in LLM confidence verbalization that can invert AUARC-based rankings, and offers a zero-cost fix (verbalization logprobs) with standardized stepwise evaluation—directly relevant to trustworthy LLM classification pipelines and security-critical reject options.

llm-security.title: What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)
llm-security.summary: The authors audit common LLM evaluation assumptions by comparing ChatGPT’s chat UI and OpenAI’s API, with and without web search, across 401 prompts from BBQ and SafetyBench and three runs per prompt, totaling 4,812 responses. Beyond accuracy, they measure response consistency, text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention, finding that chat UI was less accurate than API without search, enabling search reduced accuracy by up to 8 points and could flip modality performance trends, and repeated runs were inconsistent for up to 21% of prompts, with differing citations and abstention patterns across modalities. They conclude that relying solely on single-modality, single-run accuracy obscures important behavioral variation relevant to safety evaluations, and recommend accounting for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It highlights evaluation knobs—modality, search, and multi-run variability—that can confound safety and reliability claims for LLMs and are directly relevant to red-teaming, deployment risk assessments, and robust time-series-like benchmarking protocols.
llm-security.reason: Directly critiques common LLM benchmark assumptions (modalities, web search, API vs UI) which matters for security evaluations and red-teaming methodology and for trustworthy benchmark design.

llm-security.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
llm-security.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. Training uses an answer-verified LLM trajectory to fix a shared future, while a frozen SLM assigns counterfactual scores to candidate tokens under this common context to supervise a lightweight reranker observing only the current state and token. At inference, the LLM only expands the candidate pool and the reranker selects a single token before handing generation back to the SLM without appending any future suffix, yielding a 35.1% relative Math Avg. improvement for Qwen3-1.7B across five math reasoning benchmarks over greedy decoding.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It reframes collaboration as SLM-aware token selection, offering a practical path to safer, stronger small-model reasoning with minimal LLM involvement—relevant to alignment, tool-use gating, and cost/security tradeoffs in cooperative decoding.
llm-security.reason: FutureBridge proposes collaborative decoding between LLM and smaller models to improve SLM reasoning—relevant for efficient red-teaming, agent pipelines, and attack/defense strategies where token choice affects downstream agent behavior.

llm-security.title: DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models
llm-security.summary: The paper identifies a limitation of standard on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) in RLVR settings: it applies uniform token-level weights that ignore the temporal evolution of teacher–student divergence during autoregressive generation. It proposes DASH, which maps the deviation of each local distillation signal from the sequence-level mean to adaptive propagation gates that control backward multi-step aggregation, thereby modulating token-level supervision by the realized discrepancy sequence. Experiments on three math reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show consistent gains over matched vanilla OPSD runs without extra teacher or student forward passes, reusing existing distributions.
llm-security.why_it_matters: If you’re tuning reasoning LLMs with OPSD/RLVR, DASH offers a drop-in weighting scheme that exploits temporal divergence structure for better supervision without extra compute.
llm-security.reason: On-policy self-distillation for reasoning models improves agent reasoning and sample efficiency; relevant as a method to produce stronger agents (which affects attack surfaces and red-teaming cost), though not directly a security paper.

llm-security.title: Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Frontier Learning, which treats a library of pretrained models with mixed access regimes (black-box predictions and white-box representations) as complementary sources under distribution shift. It builds a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box models with outputs from black-box models, then trains a lightweight regularized supervised learner, guaranteeing training-sample risk no worse than any single baseline including zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, or direct training. Experiments on simulations and real-world shifts (DomainNet/VisDA and MIMIC-IV-Notes ICU mortality) show it matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy, with the largest gains when no single baseline is reliable across the shifts considered.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, access-agnostic ensemble-on-representations approach that subsumes common reuse strategies and is empirically strong under shift—relevant to robustness/security and modular reuse of foundation models.
llm-security.reason: Agentic BO using LLMs to inject priors into optimization touches on agentic systems and leveraging LLMs as components—relevant to attack/defense surfaces and efficient automated red-teaming workflows.

llm-security.title: Retrieval-Constrained Policy Optimization for Attack Technique Extraction from Cyber Threat Intelligence
llm-security.reason: Extraction of ATT&CK techniques from CTI via retrieval-constrained RL/LLM methods is relevant for security-focused information extraction and evaluation of LLMs for structured threat tasks.

adversarial-ml.title: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper studies the attack surface introduced by agent skill folders in autonomous coding agents and presents an adversarial skill-synthesis method that converts 471 real shell commands into 2,826 benign-looking skills mapped to 11 ATT&CK tactics using six LLMs. It introduces a reproducible evaluation pipeline with stratification, evidence anchoring, refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override, using a three-judge LLM panel validated against a blind human gold standard (κ=0.85). In large-scale tests (5,629 runs), Gemini CLI was exploited in 95.5–96.1% and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0% of runs with only 1.99% explicit safety recognition, and code/dataset are released at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Provides a validated benchmark, eval pipeline, and high-base-rate exploitation evidence for skill-file attacks in coding agents—directly relevant to LLM security evals and agentic deployment risk.
adversarial-ml.reason: Demonstrates pipeline attack surface in coding agents by hiding malicious shell commands in natural-language skill files — directly applicable to agentic-system attack vectors and red-teaming.

adversarial-ml.title: LoRAScan: Detecting Backdoor Prompts in Low-Rank Adapters for Large Language Models via Down-Projection Activation Spikes
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces LoRAScan, an adapter-aware defense that detects and rejects trigger-bearing inputs for potentially backdoored LoRA adapters at inference time without modifying adapter parameters. It exploits the observation that about 5% of LoRA insertion sites exhibit stable activations on clean inputs but show concentrated spikes in down-projection activations when a trigger is present; these sites are identified pre-deployment and monitored online. On standard LLM backdoor benchmarks, LoRAScan rejects approximately 98.49 of malicious inputs with a small error rate on clean inputs, outperforming existing defenses across diverse settings.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It offers a practical, deployment-compatible defense for LoRA-based supply-chain backdoors by leveraging activation signatures rather than adapter merging or retraining, aligning with current interests in robust LLM fine-tuning security.
adversarial-ml.reason: LoRAScan targets backdoored LoRA adapters—a direct supply-chain threat to LLM security (adapter-level backdoors) and practical detection method relevant to applied defenses.

adversarial-ml.title: Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models
adversarial-ml.summary: The work argues that standard NTP’s teacher-forced training is suboptimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning, and that existing MTP and NextLat objectives either have limited horizons or suffer from compounding rollout errors. It proposes Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), introducing an auxiliary higher-level abstract latent to reduce error accumulation in latent-space rollouts. Experiments indicate HiLP yields longer-horizon coherent belief state representations, improves performance on coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks, and enables more efficient speculative decoding.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: HiLP targets long-horizon error accumulation with a hierarchical latent rollout, offering a potentially practical auxiliary objective for robust reasoning and faster decoding compared to MTP/NextLat baselines.
adversarial-ml.reason: Fast, gradient-free one-shot unlearning for LLMs targets removal of sensitive data/PII and addresses practical security/privacy needs; potential for incomplete removal and attack/restore vectors makes it highly relevant.

adversarial-ml.title: The Label Defines the Timescale: Trait-State Limits of Temporal-Aggregate Learning
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper analyzes labels of temporal aggregates Θ_{g,T} built from a latent Gaussian process with a stable trait and correlated state, using an exact protocol-conditioned Bayes-risk identity. It shows label variance splits into an O(1) trait and O(T^{-1}) state component, derives task-dependent effective temporal spans (means tied to ordinary correlation time; occupation times to higher-order spectra), and proves state-driven occupation-label variance peaks at trait-threshold with window efficiency decaying slowly away from it. With a fixed segment budget, risks and simulations show repeated co-temporal segments saturate quickly while temporally dispersed observations keep improving state explainability; trait ceilings come from test-retest quantities, whereas state ceilings need short-lag calibration, implying observed limits can be protocol-driven rather than architectural.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Clarifies when snapshot protocols fundamentally cap aggregate-label predictability and how to design observation schedules to separate architectural limits from acquisition ceilings—directly relevant to security evals of LLM temporal tasks and to designing time series foundation model benchmarks.
adversarial-ml.reason: Theoretical limits on temporal-aggregate labels and protocol ceilings are relevant to time-series benchmark design and evaluation of TS foundation models and could inform realistic evaluation ceilings.

adversarial-ml.title: Bridging extrinsic and intrinsic variable importance
adversarial-ml.reason: Work on intrinsic vs extrinsic variable importance and uncertainty quantification is broadly relevant to trustworthy evaluation and interpretability methods, but not specific to LLM security or TSFM.

adversarial-ml.title: A Survey of Adversarial Efficiency Degradation for Vision Transformer by Exploiting Input-adaptive Optimization
adversarial-ml.reason: Breaks DRL-based cyber defenses via agentic red teaming — interesting for agentic threat modeling but less directly about LLM security or TS foundation models.

adversarial-ml.title: The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does
adversarial-ml.reason: Analysis of optimizer implicit bias (Adam vs GD) is relevant to robustness and training dynamics that could affect model compression/attack susceptibility, but indirect to primary interests.

tsfm.title: KReF: Training-Free Retrieval for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting and Predictive Uncertainty
tsfm.summary: KReF is a training-free retrieval framework for probabilistic long-term time-series forecasting that uses similar historical lookback–future pairs as a local empirical predictive distribution. It embeds lookbacks via handcrafted statistics or frozen random Fourier features, defines predictive masses and quantiles directly from similarity weights (also yielding CRPS and a weighted-mean point forecast), and adapts intervals using a probability-integral-transform map with validation-selected expansion/shrinkage. On six LTSF benchmarks across four horizons, KReF achieves the lowest CRPS in all 12 dataset–embedding settings and lowest IS90 in 9, with point forecasts matching or surpassing trained baselines on two datasets, and an archive-oracle analysis indicating further gains from finer routing.
tsfm.why_it_matters: Introduces a strong training-free retrieval prior for LTSF with competitive uncertainty calibration, suggesting a complementary path to learned sequence models and a retrieval-centric lens relevant to LLM/security retrieval pipelines.
tsfm.reason: Training-free retrieval for long-horizon probabilistic forecasting targets long-term TS forecasting and uncertainty without training—highly relevant to TSFM evaluation and lightweight inference approaches.

tsfm.title: Unsupervised Adaptation of PDE Foundation Models
tsfm.summary: The authors pretrain a neighborhood attention Transformer on diverse time-dependent PDEs at varying spatial scales to learn transferable representations, then adapt it to unseen equations using an unsupervised physics-based objective built from PDE residuals and boundary conditions. Adaptation uses LoRA, and they introduce NSLoRA, a Newton–Schulz orthogonalized variant to rebalance uneven learning across physical quantities. Their method matches supervised LoRA finetuning without ground-truth solutions and outperforms neural operator baselines and recent PDE foundation models across heterogeneous multi-dimensional PDE benchmarks.
tsfm.why_it_matters: Unsupervised physics-constrained finetuning with orthogonalized LoRA suggests a path to domain adaptation without labels, paralleling trends in LLM security/robustness where structure-aware, constraint-based adaptation mitigates data scarcity and uneven learning dynamics.
tsfm.reason: Unsupervised adaptation of PDE foundation models uses time-dependent PDEs and neighborhood-attention transformers for transfer without dense labels — aligns with time-series foundation model pretraining/adaptation and evaluation concerns.

tsfm.title: Diffusion LLMs as Targets and Adversaries: Mechanistic Safety Exploits
tsfm.summary: The paper studies diffusion LLMs (DLLMs) as both targets and adversaries, revealing that diffusion-based alignment is mechanistically sparse and transferable, especially when DLLMs are initialized from autoregressive models. They demonstrate direct safety neuron mapping and pruning attacks, with self-pruning boosting ASR up to 73.8%/86.6% on LLaDA/Dream and transfer pruning from Qwen2.5 boosting ASR up to 73.2%/86.3% on Dream/Fast-dLLM. They propose SN-Guided Diffusion, an offline black-box jailbreak that steers away from safety-triggering regions using a weighted safety neuron loss, achieving AUROC 1.0 for benign-vs-jailbreak discrimination and high transfer ASR on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite with only 20 generations per prompt, and release code at the linked repo.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It exposes mechanistic transfer vulnerabilities in diffusion-aligned LLMs and offers a low-cost, highly transferable black-box jailbreak method, directly informing red/blue-team defenses and mech-interp for diffusion-based architectures.
tsfm.reason: Long-horizon world-model training addresses mismatch between local losses and long-range prediction—important for long-horizon agents and TS foundation models' pretraining/objectives.

tsfm.title: Beyond Foundation Models: Dimension-Aware Neural Architecture Search with Small-Data Representation Models for Cryocooler Lifetime Prediction
tsfm.summary: The paper proposes FSD-RM, a paradigm of capacity-controlled, unsupervised representation models (CNN1D, LSTM, GRU, Transformer) for small, domain-specific time-series data, avoiding large-scale pretraining. It integrates these encoders into a two-stage pipeline for cryocooler lifetime prediction and uses dimension-aware NAS to jointly optimize model capacity and input dimensionality. Experiments on cryocooler telemetry show competitive predictive performance with reduced training cost and model complexity, enabled by explicit inductive bias and capacity control choices.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It presents a NAS-driven, small-data alternative to time-series FMs that could inform secure, resource-efficient modeling pipelines when pretraining data are scarce or restricted.
tsfm.reason: Proposes small-data representation models for time-series forecasting in domain-limited settings—directly relevant to time-series foundation-model alternatives and practical architectures.

tsfm.title: MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers
tsfm.summary: MACRO introduces a dynamic layer routing framework that treats routing over transformer layers as a context-dependent Markov policy enabling skips, repeats, and residual additions without modifying base model weights. The policy is trained with feedback on training data and decoded via a top-k Viterbi search to produce high-probability execution programs under computation budget phases and operator context. Across reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs, MACRO yields a +5.0% average accuracy over unrouted baselines, outperforms Dr. LLM by +7.2%, and reduces route-search time 9.4x (14.8→1.6 hours).
tsfm.why_it_matters: It offers a practical, label-free-at-inference routing mechanism that improves accuracy and efficiency without finetuning, relevant for secure, budget-aware deployment and compositional control of LLM computation.
tsfm.reason: Dynamic layer routing that changes execution paths without weight updates intersects with efficient inference for agents and could affect cost/behavior trade-offs in deployed LLM systems.

tsfm.title: TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting
tsfm.summary: The paper proposes TS-RAG, a retrieval-augmented approach for time series forecasting that uses specially designed reference tokens to fuse input sequences with retrieved similar sequences. It argues that naive concatenation of references, as in LLM RAG, is ineffective for typical time series models due to limited data, smaller scales, and weaker generative ability. Experiments show TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art results on several real-world forecasting benchmarks.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It bridges LLM-style RAG with time series by introducing a tailored fusion mechanism, offering a concrete path to leverage retrieval for stronger temporal forecasting without requiring LLM-scale models.
tsfm.reason: Tabular foundation model adaptation via gated skill evolution is relevant for transfer and training-free adaptation methods, but focused on tabular rather than temporal sequence models.

tsfm.title: SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models
tsfm.summary: The paper introduces SkillTFM, a training-free adaptation system for tabular foundation models that replaces parameter updates with gated evolution of agentic skills. It uses a verifiable, extensible skill bank combining boundary evidence identification to characterize task structure and base-model failures with gated skill evolution to retrieve and extend reusable skills under explicit validation. In simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142, elevating nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898, and shows effectiveness across different TFM backbones.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It proposes a security-adjacent, verifiable skill-gating mechanism for training-free adaptation under distribution shift, echoing modular skill libraries and guarded tool-use in LLMs while targeting tabular/time-series TFMs.
tsfm.reason: Empirical study of self-pretraining for medical time series—useful data on pretraining benefits and transfer in noisy, multimodal TS settings though domain-specific.

tsfm.title: Taxonomy-Driven Analysis of Open-Source AI Risk Mitigation Tools
tsfm.reason: Using VLMs to encode time-series as images speaks to practical efficiency and cross-modal approaches for time-series analysis and could impact deployment/serving costs for TS workloads.

tsfm.title: Modular TTT: Rethinking Test-Time Training as Composable Modules
tsfm.reason: Test-time training modularization is relevant to sequence-model adaptation and could inform online adaptation for time-series FMs, but paper appears more methodology-focused than directly on TSFM or security.

agents.title: When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems
agents.summary: The paper introduces PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on self-evolving skill (SES) systems that distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, where an attacker with skill-level black-box access contributes bounded evidence to influence skill promotion. It formalizes artifact poisoning as requiring Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization, identifying Attribution—making target behaviors appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable—as the key bottleneck, and demonstrates high success embedding target behaviors across six LLM evolvers in SkillClaw (91.0% SER) and transfer to Trace2Skill (61.5% SER) at 10% attacker support. Controlled studies show three consistent attacker records in a 30-record batch suffice while one is much weaker, and ablations highlight recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as main success factors, framing evidence promotion as a critical security boundary for self-evolving agents.
agents.why_it_matters: It pinpoints the promotion/attribution step in skill evolution as an attack surface with quantified vulnerability and transferable effects, informing defenses for agentic LLMs and data-driven skill distillation pipelines.
agents.reason: Robust context-aware segmentation for malicious instructions (IPI) targets detection of embedded prompt injections tailored to a query—highly relevant to defending agents and evaluating instruction-level attacks.

agents.title: Policy-Masked Private Experts: Auditable and Reversible Capability Access Control in Sparse MoE Models
agents.summary: The paper introduces Policy-Masked Private Experts, which freeze a pretrained sparse MoE, train a disjoint private expert branch, and use policy-controlled pool selection before top-k routing to ensure unauthorized requests execute no private experts under the stated TCB. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite show zero unauthorized private execution across 64 adversarial scenarios and 96 deny/fail-closed events with exact hook agreement and reversible allow-deny-allow behavior, while private branches yield significant gains on frozen Qwen benchmarks and 27.0 pp on DeepSeek, and outperform LoRA plus post-hoc gating in preventing denied adapter calls. A sealed evaluation is near-neutral, and the authors emphasize that execution control is auditable and reversible, though transfer utility remains distribution dependent.
agents.why_it_matters: It operationalizes auditable, authorization-gated capability access in sparse MoEs—relevant to LLM security and controllable specialization without degrading public behavior.
agents.reason: Capability-access controls for sparse MoE enabling auditable/reversible expert gating directly addresses attack surface and access-control mechanisms relevant to LLM security and trusted compute.

agents.title: Skill-Use: Can LLMs Actually Use Skills in Agentic Harnesses?
agents.summary: The paper introduces Skill-Use, a benchmark that tests whether LLM agents can recognize, retrieve, and apply structured skills under progressive disclosure, separating Trigger, Compliance, and Boundary facets and combining them into an SU score that only credits execution after triggering. It comprises 79 real skills and 177 executable tasks across nine domains, run in Docker sandboxes and scored via trajectory-based rubrics, and evaluates eight LLMs across two agent harnesses. Results show reliable skill use is not yet achieved (best SU 0.613), with triggering and procedural compliance as independent bottlenecks and scores/model rankings varying by harness, indicating skill use is harness-conditioned rather than an inherent model property.
agents.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, execution-grounded way to diagnose harness-conditioned failure modes (triggering vs. compliance vs. boundary) in tool-using LLM agents, informing both security-sensitive agent design and modular capability evaluation akin to time-series foundation model benchmarking.
agents.reason: Skill-Use evaluates whether agents can recognize and retrieve procedural skills under partial disclosure—directly relevant to agentic systems, tool-use security surfaces and evaluation methodology for skill-based attacks/robustness.

agents.title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
agents.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit, and performance is measured by normalized gain over the seed harness. Evaluating five frontier LLMs across four tasks and 111 runs, the authors find optimizer models differentiate more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren’t consistently superior, and gains vary substantially by task and seed regime, establishing harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with room for improvement.
agents.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, auditable setup to compare LLMs’ agentic self-improvement under realistic noisy/expensive evals—relevant for secure agent orchestration and optimizing time-series/tool-using pipelines.
agents.reason: Benchmark for optimizing agent harnesses is directly relevant to LLM agent security (attack surface via prompts/tools/orchestration) and offers an evaluation protocol useful for red-teaming and robust harness design.

agents.title: When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents
agents.summary: The paper shows that self-evolving LLM agents experience a capability-contamination phase transition: beyond a critical pool size, newly distilled skills degrade performance due to defective skills seeding cross-round contamination chains. They demonstrate structural irreversibility, where post-hoc removal of source skills recovers only a small fraction of performance, motivating pre-commit gating via Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG) with three heterogeneous critics and marginal-gain subset selection. On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation peaks then degrades with limited rollback recovery, while VaG improves every round to 72% pass@1 with a ~5x smaller pool and transfers positively to other backbones and a second benchmark, with ablations showing the critics are complementary and non-substitutable.
agents.why_it_matters: It surfaces an irreversible contamination mechanism in skill distillation and proposes a concrete pre-commit gating framework that stabilizes agent evolution and transfers across models/benchmarks, directly relevant to secure, scalable LLM agent training and model-based control of evolving skill libraries.
agents.reason: Findings about self-evolving agent skill contamination directly impact safety of agent self-improvement and distillation pipelines—important for red-teaming and mitigation strategies.

agents.title: DBLAST: Dependent Block Drafting for Stochastic Speculative Decoding
agents.summary: The paper analyzes speculative decoding with block/diffusion drafters and shows that assuming conditional independence across drafted positions breaks down under non-greedy, higher-entropy target sampling, reducing accepted draft length. It introduces DBLAST, a dependent block drafter using a low-rank latent mixture over token positions plus an acceptance-oriented objective that optimizes expected verified length. Experiments on Qwen3-4B/8B across GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks report consistent gains in accepted length over independent block sampling, particularly at higher entropy.
agents.why_it_matters: It targets stochastic decoding efficiency—key for secure, diverse sampling and alignment workflows—by improving acceptance rates under high-entropy regimes, informing both LLM safety pipelines and efficient inference design.
agents.reason: Speculative decoding for stochastic drafts impacts efficient inference for agents and could change threat surface of model outputs when combined with stochasticity — relevant to scalable red-teaming and secure deployment.

agents.title: EdgeXpert: An Edge Device for Memory-Efficient LLM Inference with Mixture-of-Experts and Speculative Decoding
agents.summary: EdgeXpert is a software-hardware co-designed LLM accelerator targeting the EMA bottleneck in FFN layers for on-device inference, combining speculative decoding with MoE despite their typical incompatibility. In prefill, it uses prompt-wise expert reuse by selecting important tokens via a lightweight encoder to build a shared expert set and routes less important tokens with a reduced expert budget to cut expert EMA; in decode, depth-aware expert coalescing loads only salient channels across same-depth speculative candidates and applies computational calibration to maintain accuracy without extra memory access. Implemented in Samsung 28nm at 800 MHz, EdgeXpert reports up to 56.3% latency and 44.1% energy reductions versus prior work while maintaining near-baseline accuracy.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a practical path to marry MoE with speculative decoding for memory-bound edge inference, yielding sizable latency/energy gains relevant to secure, private on-device LLM deployment and efficient time-sensitive workloads.
agents.reason: Skill Entropy offers a quantitative measure and training signal for cross-skill long-horizon reasoning, useful for designing and evaluating agents and long-horizon benchmarks relevant to TSFM-style sequence tasks.

agents.title: Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
agents.summary: The paper introduces Trident, an agentic LLM red-teaming framework for evaluating DRL-based cyber defenses, consisting of a dynamic benchmark across CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset of 13k+ red-blue trajectories for RLVR, and a Code-as-Policy RLVR architecture. Trident reframes red-agent training as a contextual bandit using a Log Summarizer–Planner–Coder pipeline, where a trainable Planner produces complete attack strategies from compressed logs and a frozen Coder turns them into executable Python policies against live DRL defenders. Empirically, a single 7B planner substantially degrades blue-agent performance (average 522% reduction vs. static red baselines) and uncovers emergent behaviors like decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics miss.
agents.why_it_matters: It demonstrates an RLVR-driven, code-generating agent that reliably breaks DRL cyber defenses and provides a benchmark/dataset, directly informing LLM security evaluation and agent robustness research.
agents.reason: Provides trajectory-level certification methods for modular LLM-based security agents, addressing guarantees and calibration across multi-stage pipelines — useful for safety evaluation of agentic security systems.

agents.title: DiagChain: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on Evidence-Grounded Attack Chain Reconstruction
agents.summary: DiagChain is a diagnostic benchmark for evidence-grounded attack chain reconstruction that enables stage-wise evaluation of LLM agents, addressing limits of final-output or aggregate metrics. It introduces MAIN-69 (69 scenarios across OSes, evidence noise levels, and chain lengths), an Evidence-Centric RAG approach that ties retrieval to an evolving structured chain, and five metrics targeting distinct reconstruction stages for failure diagnosis. Evaluating six LLMs, they find the strongest setup correctly reconstructs only 39.6% of 849 reference steps, with smaller models failing to integrate retrieved evidence and larger models bottlenecked by evidence ordering.
agents.why_it_matters: Offers a granular, stage-wise eval suite and methodology for security-focused LLM agents, highlighting integration vs ordering failures that current end-to-end metrics obscure.
agents.reason: Diagnostic benchmark for evidence-grounded attack chain reconstruction is relevant to evaluating LLM agents in security workflows and for stagewise failure analysis of agentic systems.

agents.title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
agents.summary: The paper introduces Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies closed-form amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase alignment to retrieved past–future windows before feeding them to a frozen TSFM. On a frozen Chronos-Bolt, it outperforms a state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter across seven benchmark datasets (average −3.75% MSE), and it also improves zero-shot MSE by 2.5%–13.7% on four additional frozen TSFMs without per-backbone tuning. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts in frozen backbones that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out futures-averaging, suggesting frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals.
agents.why_it_matters: It challenges the need for learned fusion in RAG for forecasting by showing closed-form alignment on frozen backbones yields SOTA gains and ridge-like in-context adaptation, a strong baseline relevant to LLM alignment and retrieval studies.
